docs.title: Keras Probability
docs.text:
Uncertainty awareness for deep learning in Keras 3.

keras_proba gives Keras models calibrated, distance-aware uncertainty estimates. Every layer, loss and metric runs on the TensorFlow, JAX and PyTorch backends, plugs into model.compile / model.fit, and saves with model.save.

The distance-aware and Bayesian layers are ports of TensorFlow Model Garden and TensorFlow Probability, tested for numerical parity with them.

docs.title: What's inside
docs.text: Need Use A classifier that knows when inputs are far from the training data SNGP: SpectralNormalization + RandomFeatureGaussianProcess, or the all-in-one GaussianProcessClassificationHead Uncertainty over the weights Bayesian layers: DenseFlipout, DenseReparameterization, Conv{1,2,3}DFlipout, ... Regression with a predicted noise level GaussianHead with GaussianNLL Multi-modal or skewed regression targets MixtureGaussianHead with MixtureGaussianNLL Measuring calibration ExpectedCalibrationError, BrierScore Fixing an overconfident trained classifier TemperatureScaling Intervals or sets with a coverage guarantee SplitConformalRegressor, SplitConformalClassifier

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
pip install "git+https://github.com/anas-rz/keras-proba.git"

Keras 3 needs one backend; install it with an extra, e.g. pip install "keras-proba[jax] @ git+https://github.com/anas-rz/keras-proba.git" ([torch], [jax] or [tensorflow]).

docs.title: A first example
docs.text:
A classifier whose predictions become uncertain away from the training data:

import numpy as np
import keras
import keras_proba

x = np.random.normal(size=(512, 2)).astype("float32")
y = (x[:, 0] * x[:, 1] > 0).astype("int32")

inputs = keras.Input((2,))
hidden = keras.layers.Dense(64, trainable=False)(inputs)  # A frozen random projection.
hidden = keras_proba.layers.SpectralNormalization(keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"))(hidden)
logits = keras_proba.layers.GaussianProcessClassificationHead(
    inner_dim=0,
    num_classes=2,
    temperature=np.pi / 8,
    normalize_input=False,
    scale_random_features=True,
    custom_random_features_initializer=keras.initializers.RandomNormal(stddev=1.0),
)(hidden)
model = keras.Model(inputs, logits)

model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True),
    metrics=["accuracy", keras_proba.metrics.ExpectedCalibrationError(from_logits=True)],
)
model.fit(x, y, epochs=10, verbose=0, callbacks=[keras_proba.callbacks.ResetCovarianceCallback()])

probs = keras.ops.softmax(model.predict(np.array([[0.5, 0.5], [8.0, -8.0]], "float32"), verbose=0))
# Confident near the data, close to uniform far from it.

Continue with Getting Started, or jump to a guide.

docs.title: Verified against the references
docs.text:
Each component is tested on all three backends for:

  • Parity with the original implementation (Model Garden, TensorFlow Probability, PyTorch, SciPy), feeding both the same weights and random draws.
  • Training: the method does its job on real fits, e.g. out-of-distribution uncertainty, improved calibration, or the theoretical conformal coverage.
  • Serialization: model.save / keras.models.load_model round trips.

See Testing for details, including the bugs in the references that these tests surfaced.

docs.title: Choosing your backend
docs.text:
keras_proba runs on every Keras 3 backend. Set KERAS_BACKEND before importing Keras:

PyTorchJAXTensorFlow 
import os
os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "torch"
import keras

import os
os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "jax"
import keras

import os
os.environ["KERAS_BACKEND"] = "tensorflow"
import keras

JAX and spectral normalization

In its default mode="projection", SpectralNormalization behaves like the reference only on TensorFlow and PyTorch. Use mode="reparameterization" for identical behavior on every backend; see the SNGP guide.

docs.title: From a model to calibrated uncertainty
docs.text:
A typical workflow on a classifier:

import numpy as np
import keras
from keras_proba import metrics, postprocessing

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(size=(3000, 10)).astype("float32")
y = (x[:, :3] @ rng.normal(size=(3, 4)) + rng.normal(size=(3000, 4))).argmax(-1)
(x_train, y_train), (x_cal, y_cal), (x_test, y_test) = [(x[s], y[s]) for s in (slice(0, 1500), slice(1500, 2200), slice(2200, None))]

# 1. Train, tracking calibration alongside accuracy.
model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input((10,)), keras.layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"), keras.layers.Dense(4)])
model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True),
    metrics=["accuracy", metrics.ExpectedCalibrationError(from_logits=True)],
)
model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=30, verbose=0)

# 2. Calibrate the confidence on held-out data.
scaling = postprocessing.TemperatureScaling()
scaling.fit(model.predict(x_cal, verbose=0), y_cal)
calibrated = keras.Sequential([model, scaling])

# 3. Turn predictions into sets that contain the label 90% of the time.
probs_cal = keras.ops.softmax(calibrated.predict(x_cal, verbose=0))
conformal = postprocessing.SplitConformalClassifier(alpha=0.1, score="aps").fit(y_cal, probs_cal)
sets = conformal.predict_set(keras.ops.softmax(calibrated.predict(x_test, verbose=0)))
print(float(postprocessing.set_coverage(y_test, sets)), float(postprocessing.average_set_size(sets)))

Calibration and conformal prediction work on any trained classifier. To also make the model itself uncertainty-aware, use an SNGP head or Bayesian layers.

docs.title: Saving and loading
docs.text:
Every layer, loss and metric is registered with Keras, so models save and load as usual:

calibrated.save("calibrated.keras")
restored = keras.models.load_model("calibrated.keras")

Fitted conformal predictors are plain Python objects; save them with their JSON-compatible get_config() and restore them with from_config.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
The test suite runs once per backend:

pip install -e ".[dev]"
KERAS_BACKEND=jax pytest          # Or torch, tensorflow.

docs.text: Folder What it checks tests/tests_parity Numerical parity with the original implementation, given the same weights and random draws. tests/tests_smoke Shapes, analytic values, invariants, error handling and the public API. tests/tests_training That each method does its job when trained: out-of-distribution uncertainty, improved calibration, conformal coverage of exactly \(k / (n + 1)\), ... tests/tests_serialization get_config / from_config and model.save / keras.models.load_model round trips.

docs.title: Differences from the references
docs.text:
Some deviations are deliberate, each covered by a test:

  • Brier decomposition: TFP's brier_decomposition indexes the average label distribution by the predicted class in its resolution term. keras_proba uses the textbook formula, for which uncertainty − resolution + reliability reproduces the Brier score exactly when all predictions with the same argmax are identical; TFP's can be off by up to 0.39.
  • Quantile-bucket ECE: bucket edges are data points, and TFP compares log-probabilities with edges that went through exp and log, so a point on an edge can fall in either bucket depending on float rounding. keras_proba compares in probability space, where an edge equals its data point exactly.
  • Local reparameterization: an all-zero input gives a NaN scale gradient in TFP; a tiny constant under the square root keeps it finite.
  • Spectral normalization on JAX: see the SNGP guide.
  • Robustness: the GP and SNGP head unpack every output combination (return_gp_cov=False, return_random_features=True) and accept rank-2 features, where the reference crashes.

docs.title: ResetCovarianceCallback
docs.text:
Bases: keras.src.callbacks.callback.Callback

Resets the precision matrix of every GP covariance layer at the start of each epoch.

RandomFeatureGaussianProcess accumulates its posterior precision matrix over training minibatches. Since the feature extractor changes during training, the estimate should be recomputed in each epoch, so that the final covariance only reflects the last epoch's features [1].

Example:

model.fit(x, y, epochs=10, callbacks=[ResetCovarianceCallback()])

[1]: Jeremiah Liu et al. Simple and Principled Uncertainty Estimation with Deterministic Deep Learning via Distance Awareness. In Neural Information Processing Systems, 2020. https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.10108

docs.title: RandomFourierFeatures
docs.text:
RandomFourierFeatures(output_dim, kernel_initializer='gaussian', scale=None, trainable=False, name=None, **kwargs)

Bases: keras.src.layers.layer.Layer

Projects inputs into a random feature space approximating an RBF kernel.

Typically used to "kernelize" a linear model: a linear layer trained on top of these features is (up to approximation) a kernel machine, e.g. kernel logistic regression or the random feature Gaussian process used in SNGP.

Example:

model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.Input(shape=(784,)),
    RandomFourierFeatures(output_dim=4096, scale=10.0),
    keras.layers.Dense(10, activation="softmax"),
])

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default output_dim

Positive integer, the number of random features D.

required kernel_initializer

"gaussian", "laplacian" (case insensitive), or a Keras initializer for the random feature kernel W. The kernel is never trainable.

'gaussian' scale

Positive float, the kernel length scale. If None, defaults to sqrt(input_dim / 2) for "gaussian" and 1.0 otherwise. If trainable=True, it is learned and this is its initial value.

None trainable

Whether scale is trainable. Defaults to False.

False name

String, name of the layer.

None Input shape

(..., input_dim) with a defined last dimension. Unlike the reference, inputs of rank greater than 2 are supported.

Output shape

(..., output_dim).

docs.text:
RandomFeatureGaussianProcess(units, num_inducing=1024, gp_kernel_type='gaussian', gp_kernel_scale=1.0, gp_output_bias=0.0, normalize_input=False, gp_kernel_scale_trainable=False, gp_output_bias_trainable=False, gp_cov_momentum=0.999, gp_cov_ridge_penalty=1.0, scale_random_features=True, use_custom_random_features=True, custom_random_features_initializer=None, custom_random_features_activation=None, l2_regularization=1e-06, gp_cov_likelihood='gaussian', return_gp_cov=True, return_random_features=False, dtype=None, name=None, trainable=True, **gp_output_kwargs)

Bases: keras.src.layers.layer.Layer

Gaussian process layer with random feature approximation [1].

During training, the layer updates the maximum a posteriori (MAP) logits and the posterior precision matrix using minibatch statistics. During inference, it also returns the predictive covariance, which can be used to compute posterior mean probabilities via mean_field_logits.

Different random features can be used by setting use_custom_random_features=True and changing the initializer and activation of the custom random features. For example:

MLP kernel: initializer="random_normal", activation="relu"
RBF kernel: initializer="random_normal", activation=keras.ops.cos

A linear kernel can be used with gp_kernel_type="linear" and use_custom_random_features=True.

Example:

inputs = keras.Input(shape=(128,))
logits, covmat = RandomFeatureGaussianProcess(units=10)(inputs)
probs = keras.ops.softmax(mean_field_logits(logits, covmat, math.pi / 8))

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default units

Number of output units.

required num_inducing

Number of random Fourier features.

1024 gp_kernel_type

Kernel type. "gaussian" (RBF) by default, or "linear" when use_custom_random_features=True.

'gaussian' gp_kernel_scale

Length scale of the kernel, i.e. for the RBF kernel exp(-|x1 - x2|**2 / gp_kernel_scale).

1.0 gp_output_bias

Initial value of the output bias.

0.0 normalize_input

Whether to apply layer normalization to the input.

False gp_kernel_scale_trainable

Whether the length scale is trainable. Only used when use_custom_random_features=False.

False gp_output_bias_trainable

Whether the output bias is trainable.

False gp_cov_momentum

Discount factor of the moving average of the precision matrix. If not positive, minibatch precision matrices are summed instead, which gives the exact precision after one pass over the data.

Whether to scale random features by sqrt(2 / num_inducing).

LaplaceRandomFeatureCovariance(momentum=0.999, ridge_penalty=1.0, likelihood='gaussian', dtype=None, name=None, **kwargs)

Bases: keras.src.layers.layer.Layer

Computes the Gaussian process covariance using the Laplace method.

At training time, this layer updates the Gaussian process posterior using model features in minibatches.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default momentum

Discount factor of the moving average of the posterior precision matrix, analogous to batch normalization momentum. If not positive, minibatch precision matrices are summed instead, which gives the exact precision matrix after one pass over the data (e.g. in the final epoch).

0.999 ridge_penalty

Ridge penalty of the initial precision matrix. It stabilizes the inverse inv(t(X) X + s I), but should not be so large that it dominates t(X) X.

1.0 likelihood

Likelihood used for the Laplace approximation, one of "gaussian", "binary_logistic" or "poisson".

'gaussian' Call arguments

inputs: GP random features of shape (batch_size, num_features). logits: Pre-activation output of shape (batch_size, 1). Required for non-Gaussian likelihoods. training: Whether to update the precision matrix.

Returns:

Type Description

Identity of shape (batch_size, batch_size) during training, and the

predictive covariance of the same shape during inference.

docs.title: compute_predictive_covariance
docs.text:
compute_predictive_covariance(gp_feature)

Computes the posterior predictive covariance.

Given training random features Phi_tr of shape (num_train, num_hidden) and test random features Phi_ts of shape (batch_size, num_hidden), the predictive covariance (assuming a Gaussian likelihood) is:

s * Phi_ts @ inv(t(Phi_tr) * Phi_tr + s * I) @ t(Phi_ts),

where s is the ridge penalty used to stabilize the inverse.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default gp_feature

Random features of the test data, shape (batch_size, num_hidden).

required

Returns:

Type Description

Predictive covariance matrix of shape (batch_size, batch_size).

update_weights(training=True)

Runs power iteration and bounds the kernel's spectral norm.

With training=True, u and v are updated by power iteration first. Otherwise the current u and v are used as is.

In "projection" mode, the normalized kernel is assigned to the wrapped layer. Unlike the reference, which uses the raw kernel at inference, this keeps inference normalized on JAX; elsewhere it is a no-op unless the kernel changed since the last training call. In "reparameterization" mode, the kernel is left unchanged.

Returns:

Type Description

The normalized kernel.

Bases: keras_proba.layers.classification_head.ClassificationHead

Gaussian process-based pooling head for classification (SNGP) [1].

It applies spectral normalization to the hidden pooler layer, and replaces the dense output layer with a random feature Gaussian process. During training it returns the raw logits; at inference it returns logits adjusted with mean_field_logits, and optionally the covariance matrix.

Remember to reset the GP covariance at the start of each epoch, e.g. with keras_proba.callbacks.ResetCovarianceCallback.

Example:

inputs = keras.Input((128,))
hidden = keras.layers.Dense(128, activation="relu")(inputs)
head = GaussianProcessClassificationHead(inner_dim=128, num_classes=10, temperature=math.pi / 8)
model = keras.Model(inputs, head(hidden))

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default inner_dim

Dimensionality of the inner projection layer. If 0 or None, only the output projection layer is created.

required num_classes

Number of output classes.

required cls_token_idx

Index of the sequence position to pool when the input has rank 3.

0 activation

Activation of the inner projection layer.

'tanh' dropout_rate

Dropout probability before the output projection.

0.0 initializer

Initializer for the dense layer kernels.

'glorot_uniform' use_spec_norm

Whether to apply spectral normalization to the pooler layer.

True use_gp_layer

Whether to use a Gaussian process as the output layer.

True temperature

Mean-field factor used at inference. If None, no mean-field adjustment is applied.

None **kwargs

Spectral normalization arguments (iteration, norm_multiplier, mode), RandomFeatureGaussianProcess arguments (see extract_gp_layer_kwargs for those supported and their defaults), and keyword arguments for keras.layers.Layer.

required Call arguments

features: Tensor of shape (batch_size, seq_len, hidden_size) or (batch_size, hidden_size). training: Whether the layer is in training mode. return_covmat: Whether to also return the covariance matrix of shape (batch_size, batch_size) when use_gp_layer=True. During training, keep it False to be compatible with model.fit().

])
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True))

Name Type Description Default units

required activation

None use_bias

Initializer for the posterior mean of the kernel. Defaults to RandomNormal(stddev=0.1).

None kernel_untransformed_scale_initializer

Initializer for the posterior scale before softplus. Defaults to RandomNormal(mean=-3, stddev=0.1), a posterior close to a point mass.

None bias_initializer

Initializer for the bias. Defaults to RandomNormal(stddev=0.1).

None kernel_prior_scale

Standard deviation of the Normal kernel prior.

1.0 kl_weight

Multiplier of the KL divergence added to the losses, e.g. 1 / num_train_examples.

1.0 seed

Seed for the random noise.

docs.title: expected_calibration_error_quantiles
docs.text:
expected_calibration_error_quantiles(hit, pred_log_prob, num_buckets=20, axis=0, log_space_buckets=False)

Expected calibration error over equal-count buckets of predicted probability.

A model is calibrated if buckets of predicted probabilities have the same within-bucket average accuracy. The ECE is the average absolute difference between predicted probability and bucket accuracy:

bucket_weight = bucket_count / sum(bucket_count)
bucket_error = abs(bucket_accuracy - bucket_confidence)
ece = sum(bucket_weight * bucket_error)

where buckets are num_buckets-quantiles of exp(pred_log_prob).

Example:

hit = [False, False, True, False, True, True]
log_pred = np.log([0.1, 0.05, 0.5, 0.2, 0.99, 0.99])
ece, acc, conf, cnt, edges, bucket = expected_calibration_error_quantiles(hit, log_pred, num_buckets=3)
# ece  ==> 0.145
# acc  ==> [0., 0., 1.]
# conf ==> [0.075, 0.2, 0.826665]
# cnt  ==> [2., 1., 3.]

For a probability vector p and a realized outcome k, the Brier score is sum_i p[i]^2 - 2 p[k]. Smaller values are better. It is a strictly proper scoring rule, and can be negative. This form differs from sum_i (p[i] - onehot(k)[i])^2 by a constant of 1.

docs.title: brier_decomposition
docs.text:
brier_decomposition(labels, logits)

Decomposes the Brier score into uncertainty, resolution, and reliability.

Any proper scoring rule admits a unique decomposition as Score = Uncertainty - Resolution + Reliability, where:

  • Uncertainty is a generalized entropy of the average predictive distribution; it can be positive or negative.
  • Resolution is a generalized variance of individual predictive distributions; it is always non-negative, and larger is better.
  • Reliability measures calibration of predictions against the true frequency of events; it is always non-negative, and lower is better.

The space of predictive distributions is discretized by their argmax. The estimation error of each component is O(k/n) for n instances and k labels.

Note: TFP's implementation computes the resolution as sum_k w_k sum_j (pbar[k] - dist_mean[k, j])^2, indexing the average label distribution by the predicted class. Here it is sum_k w_k sum_j (pbar[j] - dist_mean[k, j])^2, for which the decomposition reproduces the Brier score exactly when all predictions with the same argmax are identical. Uncertainty and reliability match TFP.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default labels

Integer tensor of shape (..., n) with class labels.

required logits

Tensor of shape (..., n, num_classes).

required

Returns:

Type Description

Tuple of uncertainty, resolution and reliability, each of shape

(...).

SplitConformalRegressor(alpha=0.1)

Split conformal prediction intervals for regression.

Without scale, the score is the absolute residual |y - y_pred| and intervals have a constant width 2 q_hat. With a per-example scale (e.g. the standard deviation of a GaussianHead, MixtureGaussianHead or Monte Carlo samples), the score is |y - y_pred| / scale and intervals y_pred +- q_hat * scale adapt to each input [2]. Each output dimension gets its own threshold, so coverage holds for each dimension separately.

Example:

mean, scale = split_gaussian_params(model.predict(x_cal))
conformal = SplitConformalRegressor(alpha=0.1).fit(y_cal, mean, scale=scale)
mean, scale = split_gaussian_params(model.predict(x_test))
lower, upper = conformal.predict_interval(mean, scale=scale)

    (e.g. the standard deviation of a `GaussianHead`, `MixtureGaussianHead` or
    Monte Carlo samples), the score is `|y - y_pred| / scale` and intervals
    `y_pred +- q_hat * scale` adapt to each input [2]. Each output dimension
    gets its own threshold, so coverage holds for each dimension separately.

    Example:

    ```python
    mean, scale = split_gaussian_params(model.predict(x_cal))
    conformal = SplitConformalRegressor(alpha=0.1).fit(y_cal, mean, scale=scale)
    mean, scale = split_gaussian_params(model.predict(x_test))
    lower, upper = conformal.predict_interval(mean, scale=scale)
    ```

    Args:
        alpha: Miscoverage level in `(0, 1)`; intervals cover with probability
            at least `1 - alpha`.
    '

SplitConformalClassifier(alpha=0.1, score='lac', from_logits=False, randomized=True, seed=None)

Split conformal prediction sets for classification.

Scores:

  • "lac" (least ambiguous set-valued classifier): 1 - p_label. Sets are {k : p_k >= 1 - q_hat}, with exact coverage and the smallest average size [2]; they can be empty for ambiguous inputs.

percentile(x, q, axis=None, interpolation=None, keepdims=False)

Computes the q-th percentile(s) of x.

Given a vector x, the q-th percentile is the value q / 100 of the way from the minimum to the maximum in a sorted copy of x. The two nearest neighbors and interpolation determine the result when the normalized rank does not match a sample exactly. Compare to numpy.percentile.

Example:

x = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]

percentile(x, q=30.0, interpolation="linear")  # 1.9
percentile(x, q=[30.0, 70.0], interpolation="lower")  # [1.0, 3.0]
percentile([[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]], q=100.0, axis=[0])  # [3.0, 4.0]

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default x

Numeric tensor with at least one dimension.

required q

Scalar or 1-D percentile(s) in [0, 100], as concrete values.

required axis

None interpolation

One of "nearest" (default), "linear", "lower", "higher" or "midpoint", used when a percentile lies between samples i < j: i + (j - i) * fraction, i, j, the nearest of the two, or (i + j) / 2. "linear" and "midpoint" require a floating point x.

False

docs.title: Bayesian layers
docs.text:
Bayesian layers learn a distribution over their weights instead of a point estimate, with variational inference 1. Their predictions are stochastic: averaging several of them gives the predictive mean, and their spread is the model's (epistemic) uncertainty.

The layers are ports of TensorFlow Probability's tfp.layers, with its default distributions:

  • Posterior: a mean-field Normal \(q(W) = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma = \epsilon + \mathrm{softplus}(\rho)\), initialized close to a point mass.
  • Prior: \(p(W) = \mathcal{N}(0, s^2)\) with kernel_prior_scale \(= s\) (default 1).
  • Bias: a point estimate.

Each call samples a kernel and adds kl_weight * KL(q(W) || p(W)) to the layer's losses, which model.fit adds to the training loss.

docs.title: Estimators
docs.text: Layers Estimator Notes DenseReparameterization, Conv{1,2,3}DReparameterization Reparameterization 2 One kernel sample per call, shared by the batch. DenseLocalReparameterization Local reparameterization 3 Samples the pre-activations directly, independently per example. DenseFlipout, Conv{1,2,3}DFlipout Flipout 4 Pseudo-independent perturbations per example with random signs: lower gradient variance, about twice the compute.

docs.title: Setting kl_weight
docs.text:
With the default mean loss over examples, the KL term must be counted once per epoch: set kl_weight = 1 / num_train_examples. With kl_weight=1 (the TFP default), the prior dominates and the posterior stays close to it.

import numpy as np
import keras
from keras_proba import layers

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.uniform(-2, 2, size=(512, 1)).astype("float32")
y = (np.sin(2 * x) + rng.normal(size=(512, 1)) * 0.1).astype("float32")

kl_weight = 1.0 / len(x)
model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.Input((1,)),
    layers.DenseFlipout(64, activation="relu", kl_weight=kl_weight),
    layers.DenseFlipout(64, activation="relu", kl_weight=kl_weight),
    layers.DenseFlipout(1, kl_weight=kl_weight),
])
model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(0.01), loss="mse")
model.fit(x, y, epochs=20, batch_size=64, verbose=0)

docs.title: Monte Carlo prediction
docs.text:
Every predict call draws fresh weights, on every backend, so the predictive distribution is a loop away:

x_test = np.linspace(-4, 4, 50, dtype="float32")[:, None]
samples = np.stack([model.predict(x_test, verbose=0) for _ in range(30)])
mean, epistemic_std = samples.mean(0), samples.std(0)  # The spread grows outside [-2, 2].

Pass seed= to a layer for reproducible samples.

docs.title: Convolutions
docs.text:
Conv1D, Conv2D and Conv3D variants take the usual filters, kernel_size, strides, padding ("valid" or "same"), data_format and dilation_rate:

model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.Input((28, 28, 1)),
    layers.Conv2DFlipout(16, 3, padding="same", activation="relu", kl_weight=1e-4),
    keras.layers.MaxPooling2D(),
    keras.layers.Flatten(),
    layers.DenseFlipout(10, kl_weight=1e-4),
])

Differences from TFP

  • The posterior and prior are fixed to TFP's defaults and configured with plain arguments, instead of arbitrary tfd distribution functions.
  • kl_weight replaces passing a custom divergence function to scale the KL term.
  • DenseLocalReparameterization adds the smallest positive float under its square root: in TFP, an all-zero input (e.g. after a ReLU) makes the scale gradient NaN.

  1. Charles Blundell et al. Weight Uncertainty in Neural Networks. ICML 2015. ↩

  2. Diederik Kingma, Max Welling. Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes. ICLR 2014. ↩

  3. Diederik Kingma, Tim Salimans, Max Welling. Variational Dropout and the Local Reparameterization Trick. NeurIPS 2015. ↩

  4. Yeming Wen et al. Flipout: Efficient Pseudo-Independent Weight Perturbations on Mini-Batches. ICLR 2018. ↩

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text: A classifier is calibrated when its confidence matches its accuracy: among predictions made with 80% confidence, 80% are correct. Modern networks are often overconfident 1.

docs.title: Measuring calibration
docs.text:
ExpectedCalibrationError bins predictions by confidence and averages the gap between confidence and accuracy per bin; BrierScore is a proper scoring rule for the whole predicted distribution. Both accumulate over batches, so evaluate gives the value on the whole dataset:

import numpy as np
import keras
from keras_proba import metrics, postprocessing

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.normal(size=(2300, 10)).astype("float32")
y = (1.5 * x[:, :3] + rng.gumbel(size=(2300, 3))).argmax(-1)
(x_train, y_train), (x_val, y_val), (x_test, y_test) = (x[:300], y[:300]), (x[300:1300], y[300:1300]), (x[1300:], y[1300:])

model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input((10,)), keras.layers.Dense(128, activation="relu"), keras.layers.Dense(3)])
model.compile(
    optimizer="adam",
    loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True),
    metrics=[metrics.ExpectedCalibrationError(num_bins=15, from_logits=True), metrics.BrierScore(from_logits=True)],
)
model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=100, verbose=0)  # Overfits, so becomes overconfident.
print(model.evaluate(x_test, y_test, verbose=0, return_dict=True))

The metrics take probabilities or logits (from_logits), sparse or one-hot labels, and a single sigmoid output for binary classification. The functions expected_calibration_error, expected_calibration_error_quantiles (equal-count bins) and brier_decomposition (uncertainty, resolution and reliability) evaluate a full set of predictions at once.

docs.title: Temperature scaling
docs.text:
TemperatureScaling divides the logits of a trained model by a single temperature \(T\), fitted to minimize the negative log-likelihood on held-out data. It changes the confidence, never the predicted class:

scaling = postprocessing.TemperatureScaling()
temperature = scaling.fit(model.predict(x_val, verbose=0), y_val)  # > 1 for an overconfident model.
calibrated = keras.Sequential([model, scaling])
calibrated.compile(
    loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True),
    metrics=[metrics.ExpectedCalibrationError(num_bins=15, from_logits=True)],
)
print(temperature, calibrated.evaluate(x_test, y_test, verbose=0, return_dict=True))

fit finds the exact optimum: the NLL is convex in \(1 / T\), so it is minimized by bisection in float64, with the same result on every backend and no learning rate to tune. The layer can also be trained with model.fit on a model whose other layers are frozen.

  1. Chuan Guo, Geoff Pleiss, Yu Sun, Kilian Q. Weinberger. On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks. ICML 2017. arXiv:1706.04599 ↩

docs.title: Conformal prediction
docs.text:
Split conformal prediction 1 2 turns any trained model into one with prediction intervals (regression) or prediction sets (classification) that contain the true label with probability at least \(1 - \alpha\). The only assumption is that calibration and test examples are exchangeable, e.g. drawn from the same distribution.

  1. Compute a nonconformity score \(s_i\) for each of \(n\) held-out calibration examples.
  2. Take \(\hat{q}\), the \(k\)-th smallest score, with \(k = \lceil (n + 1)(1 - \alpha) \rceil\).
  3. For a test input, return every label whose score is at most \(\hat{q}\).

The expected coverage is then exactly \(k / (n + 1)\) for continuous scores, between \(1 - \alpha\) and \(1 - \alpha + 1 / (n + 1)\).

The exact order statistic

keras_proba uses the \(k\)-th smallest score. The widely used numpy.quantile(scores, k / n, method="higher") selects the next larger one, which over-covers.

docs.title: Regression
docs.text:
SplitConformalRegressor uses absolute residuals \(|y - \hat{y}|\), giving intervals of constant width:

import numpy as np
import keras
from keras_proba import layers, losses, ops, postprocessing

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.uniform(-3, 3, size=(4000, 1)).astype("float32")
y = (np.sin(x) + rng.normal(size=x.shape) * (0.1 + 0.4 * np.abs(x))).astype("float32")
(x_train, y_train), (x_cal, y_cal), (x_test, y_test) = [(x[s], y[s]) for s in (slice(0, 2000), slice(2000, 3000), slice(3000, None))]

model = keras.Sequential([keras.Input((1,)), keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"), layers.GaussianHead(1)])
model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(0.005), loss=losses.GaussianNLL())
model.fit(x_train, y_train, epochs=20, batch_size=128, verbose=0)
mean_cal, scale_cal = ops.split_gaussian_params(model.predict(x_cal, verbose=0))
mean_test, scale_test = ops.split_gaussian_params(model.predict(x_test, verbose=0))

conformal = postprocessing.SplitConformalRegressor(alpha=0.1).fit(y_cal, mean_cal)
lower, upper = conformal.predict_interval(mean_test)
print(float(postprocessing.interval_coverage(y_test, lower, upper)[0]))  # ~0.9

With a per-example scale, the score is the normalized residual \(|y - \hat{y}| / \sigma\), and the intervals \(\hat{y} \pm \hat{q} \sigma\) adapt to each input: narrow where the noise is low, wide where it is high. The scale can come from a GaussianHead, a MixtureGaussianHead (ops.mixture_mean_and_stddev) or the spread of Monte Carlo samples of a Bayesian model:

conformal = postprocessing.SplitConformalRegressor(alpha=0.1).fit(y_cal, mean_cal, scale=scale_cal)
lower, upper = conformal.predict_interval(mean_test, scale=scale_test)

Each output dimension gets its own threshold, so coverage holds for each dimension.

docs.title: Classification
docs.text:
SplitConformalClassifier returns boolean prediction sets of shape (n, num_classes), with two scores:

score Sets Properties "lac" Classes with probability at least \(1 - \hat{q}\) Exact coverage and the smallest sets on average; can be empty for ambiguous inputs. "aps" 3 The most probable classes until their mass reaches \(\hat{q}\) Set size adapts to each input's difficulty. Randomized by default for exact coverage (set seed= for reproducibility). 
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
x = rng.normal(size=(3000, 2)).astype("float32")
y = (x @ rng.normal(size=(2, 5)) + rng.gumbel(size=(3000, 5))).argmax(-1)
classifier = keras.Sequential([keras.Input((2,)), keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"), keras.layers.Dense(5, activation="softmax")])
classifier.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy")
classifier.fit(x[:2000], y[:2000], epochs=10, verbose=0)
probs_cal, probs_test = classifier.predict(x[2000:2500], verbose=0), classifier.predict(x[2500:], verbose=0)

conformal = postprocessing.SplitConformalClassifier(alpha=0.1, score="aps", seed=0).fit(y[2000:2500], probs_cal)
sets = conformal.predict_set(probs_test)
print(float(postprocessing.set_coverage(y[2500:], sets)), float(postprocessing.average_set_size(sets)))

Non-randomized APS

randomized=False gives the classic non-randomized APS sets, which are never empty but conservative. On a hard 5-class task (63% accuracy) with a 90% target, they covered 99.6% of labels with 3.7 classes per set, against 90.0% and 2.2 classes for randomized APS.

docs.title: Probabilistic regression
docs.text: A regression model trained with mean squared error predicts a single value. A probabilistic regression head predicts a distribution per input, so the model also learns how noisy each target is (aleatoric uncertainty), and it is trained by maximum likelihood.

docs.title: Gaussian head
docs.text:
GaussianHead predicts a mean and a standard deviation per output 1 2: \(y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu(x), \sigma(x)^2)\) with $\sigma = \mathrm{softplus}(\cdot) + $ min_scale. Its output is [mean, scale] concatenated on the last axis, so it trains with plain targets and GaussianNLL:

import numpy as np
import keras
from keras_proba import layers, losses, ops

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.uniform(-3, 3, size=(2048, 1)).astype("float32")
noise_std = 0.05 + 0.3 * np.abs(x)  # The noise grows with |x|.
y = (np.sin(x) + rng.normal(size=x.shape) * noise_std).astype("float32")

model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.Input((1,)),
    keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
    keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
    layers.GaussianHead(1),
])
model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(0.005), loss=losses.GaussianNLL())
model.fit(x, y, epochs=20, batch_size=128, verbose=0)

mean, scale = ops.split_gaussian_params(model.predict(x[:5], verbose=0))

The predicted scale tracks the true noise level, and mean ± 1.96 * scale is a 95% interval. For intervals with a guaranteed coverage, pass mean and scale to a conformal regressor.

docs.title: Mixture density network
docs.text:
A single Gaussian cannot represent targets with several modes, e.g. \(y = \pm x^2\). MixtureGaussianHead predicts a mixture of num_components Gaussians 3:

\[p(y \mid x) = \sum_k \pi_k(x) \prod_d \mathcal{N}(y_d; \mu_{kd}(x), \sigma_{kd}(x)^2)\] 
sign = np.where(rng.uniform(size=x.shape) < 0.5, -1.0, 1.0)
y_bimodal = (sign * x**2 + rng.normal(size=x.shape) * 0.1).astype("float32")

model = keras.Sequential([
    keras.Input((1,)),
    keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
    keras.layers.Dense(64, activation="relu"),
    layers.MixtureGaussianHead(num_components=3),
])
model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(0.005), loss=losses.MixtureGaussianNLL())
model.fit(x, y_bimodal, epochs=20, batch_size=128, verbose=0)

params = model.predict(x[:5], verbose=0)
logits, means, scales = ops.split_mixture_params(params)  # (5, 3), (5, 3, 1), (5, 3, 1).
mean, stddev = ops.mixture_mean_and_stddev(params)  # Including the spread between components.

Training mixtures

Mixtures can get stuck covering only some of the modes. In our tests, tanh hidden layers at a learning rate of 0.005 saturated and missed a mode in about half the runs, while ReLU features recovered both modes in every run. Prefer ReLU-like features or a small learning rate.

The mixture NLL sums the log-densities of a multi-output target (its joint likelihood), while GaussianNLL averages them over outputs; they agree for one output and one component.

  1. David A. Nix, Andreas S. Weigend. Estimating the mean and variance of the target probability distribution. ICNN 1994. ↩

  2. Balaji Lakshminarayanan, Alexander Pritzel, Charles Blundell. Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles. NeurIPS 2017. ↩

  3. Christopher M. Bishop. Mixture Density Networks. Technical report, Aston University, 1994. ↩

docs.title: Distance-aware models (SNGP)
docs.text:
The Spectral-normalized Neural Gaussian Process (SNGP) 1 makes a deterministic network aware of the distance between a test input and its training data, so its predictions become uncertain away from the data. It needs two changes to a standard network:

  1. Spectral normalization of the hidden layers, so that distances in input space are preserved in feature space (the network is bi-Lipschitz).
  2. A Gaussian process output layer instead of a dense layer, whose predictive variance grows with the distance from the training features.

The layers are ports of TensorFlow Model Garden's official/nlp/modeling/layers.

docs.title: The Gaussian process output layer
docs.text:
RandomFeatureGaussianProcess approximates a GP with random Fourier features 2, \(\phi(x) = \sqrt{2 / D} \cos(x W + b)\), followed by a linear layer. During training it accumulates the posterior precision matrix of the output weights over minibatches (the Laplace approximation); at inference it also returns the predictive covariance:

import numpy as np
import keras
from keras_proba import callbacks, layers, ops

inputs = keras.Input((16,))
logits, covmat = layers.RandomFeatureGaussianProcess(units=3, num_inducing=256)(inputs)
model = keras.Model(inputs, [logits, covmat])

x = np.random.normal(size=(8, 16)).astype("float32")
logits, covmat = model.predict(x, verbose=0)  # (8, 3) and (8, 8).

# Uncertainty-adjusted logits: the mean-field approximation of the posterior predictive.
adjusted = ops.mean_field_logits(logits, covmat, mean_field_factor=np.pi / 8)

The covariance is an estimate over the features seen during training. Because the features change while the network trains, reset it at the start of every epoch, so that the final estimate only reflects the last epoch:

train_model = keras.Model(inputs, model.outputs[0])
train_model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True))
train_model.fit(x, np.zeros(8), epochs=2, verbose=0, callbacks=[callbacks.ResetCovarianceCallback()])

ResetCovarianceCallback finds every covariance layer in the model, including those nested in other layers. With gp_cov_momentum=-1, the precision matrix is the exact sum over one epoch instead of a moving average.

docs.title: Spectral normalization
docs.text:
SpectralNormalization wraps a Dense layer (and SpectralNormalizationConv2D a Conv2D) and bounds the spectral norm of its kernel by norm_multiplier, estimated with power iteration. It has two modes:

mode Training rule Backends "projection" (default) The kernel is projected to the norm bound before each step, as in the reference. Identical to the reference on TensorFlow and PyTorch. On JAX, assignments to trainable variables inside fit are discarded, so the projected kernel is not persisted between steps; a warning is shown. "reparameterization" The layer is called with \(W \cdot c / \sigma(W)\) and the gradient flows through \(\sigma\), as in PyTorch's spectral_norm. The kernel variable is never modified. Identical on every backend.

In both modes, inference uses a normalized kernel on every backend.

docs.title: The SNGP classification head
docs.text:
GaussianProcessClassificationHead combines both: a spectral-normalized pooling layer and a GP output layer. It returns raw logits during training (compatible with model.fit) and mean-field adjusted logits at inference (temperature is the mean-field factor). Pass return_covmat=True to also get the covariance.

The defaults are tuned for BERT features

The head's defaults follow the reference, which was designed for BERT encoders: a tanh pooler, layer normalization of the GP input and random features with a standard deviation of 0.05. On small dense inputs, these hide the distance from the data: in our tests, out-of-distribution confidence stayed at 0.77 to 0.98. For such inputs, use the setup of the SNGP paper: a distance-preserving backbone and

head = layers.GaussianProcessClassificationHead(
    inner_dim=0,                  # No tanh pooler.
    num_classes=2,
    normalize_input=False,        # Keep the input magnitude.
    scale_random_features=True,
    custom_random_features_initializer=keras.initializers.RandomNormal(stddev=1.0),
    temperature=np.pi / 8,
    mode="reparameterization",
)

docs.title: A complete recipe
docs.text:
A distance-preserving backbone (a frozen random projection and residual spectral-normalized blocks) with the head:

from keras_proba import layers

def build_sngp(num_classes, hidden=64, blocks=2):
    inputs = keras.Input((2,))
    h = keras.layers.Dense(hidden, trainable=False)(inputs)
    for _ in range(blocks):
        block = layers.SpectralNormalization(
            keras.layers.Dense(hidden, activation="relu"), norm_multiplier=0.9, mode="reparameterization"
        )
        h = h + block(h)
    logits = layers.GaussianProcessClassificationHead(
        inner_dim=0,
        num_classes=num_classes,
        num_inducing=1024,
        normalize_input=False,
        scale_random_features=True,
        custom_random_features_initializer=keras.initializers.RandomNormal(stddev=1.0),
        temperature=np.pi / 8,
        gp_cov_momentum=-1,
    )(h)
    return keras.Model(inputs, logits)

model = build_sngp(num_classes=2)
model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(0.01), loss=keras.losses.SparseCategoricalCrossentropy(from_logits=True))

On a two-moons dataset this reaches about 99% confidence in distribution, and 0.55 to 0.73 far from the data (0.5 is uniform), on every backend.
